232.title: Up the mountain (Matthew 5:1–2)
232.hook: he sits down, the way a rabbi teaches, and opens his mouth
232.howItsDone: Parts of the Sermon on the Mount come up in church readings through the year, and some Christians read all three chapters at once, slowly, as a whole.

segments.voice: Yesterday, beginning, back to Galilee, and your line was start again, knowing more. Now camp five: the depths.

A speaker stops pacing. Pulls up a chair. Sits down. The room goes quiet, because something is about to be said. The path now goes somewhere new: the Sermon on the Mount, chapters five, six and seven of Matthew's Gospel. A long block of Jesus's teaching, full of lines people still quote, often without knowing where they come from. Blessed are the meek. Turn the other cheek. Salt and light. The Lord's Prayer. Treasure where moth and rust corrupt. The house on the rock. And Matthew sets the scene in just two verses.
screen: `A SPEAKER SITS DOWN.` → `MATTHEW 5 TO 7.` → `LINES PEOPLE STILL QUOTE.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the King James Bible: "And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him: And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying." Three small details, each one doing something. First, he went up into a mountain. Some readers hear an echo of Moses, who went up Sinai and came down with the law: here's a new teacher on a mountain, giving teaching about how to live. Matthew never names the mountain. Tradition places it on a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum, and a church stands there today. Second, when he was set: when he sat down. Today a speaker stands to show authority. In his world, a teacher sat. Jesus sits down in the synagogue at Nazareth to teach, and later speaks of teachers who sit in Moses' seat. Sitting down means class is in session. Third, he opened his mouth. It sounds redundant; how else would he speak? But some readers hear a solemn way of saying, what follows is weighty, like saying, and he began. Luke has a shorter version of some of the same teaching, set on a level place, and some readers think Jesus taught these sayings more than once. Either way, the posture is the point. Before the disciples hear a single word, they come close. The sermon's first move isn't doing anything. It's coming near and listening.
screen: `HE WENT UP INTO A MOUNTAIN.` · `WHEN HE WAS SET: HE SAT DOWN.` · `HE OPENED HIS MOUTH.` · `THE DISCIPLES CAME NEAR.` · then, large: `AND HE OPENED HIS MOUTH, AND TAUGHT THEM.`

segments.voice: Sit, if you're not already, let your feet rest on the ground, and put your phone face down. For these two minutes, don't answer, fix or plan anything; just listen, to the room, to your breath, to what's underneath the noise. If you pray, you can come near, the way the disciples did, and let God speak first.
Moses, the echo some readers hear: as he went up Sinai, Jesus goes up a mountain too, and sits down the way a teacher did.
Your line: sit down, listen. The first words of the sermon come next. See you tomorrow.

the prophet Elijah, who heard God on a mountain
the disciple who first climbed up to sit near Jesus

233.title: The poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3)
233.hook: blessed are the poor in spirit: the empty-handed have room for the kingdom
233.howItsDone: Some Christians know the Beatitudes by heart; Orthodox churches often sing them in the Divine Liturgy, and a number of churches read them on All Saints' Day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus went up the mountain and sat down, an echo of Moses, and your line was sit down, listen.

Hashtag blessed. You've seen it under photos of a new car, a beach, a baby, a promotion. Blessed means things are going well. Back on that hillside, crowds have followed Jesus from all over, bringing their sick. He has just sat down. And the first words of the sermon are a list of people who are blessed. Only nobody on the list has a new car. It starts with the people who have nothing.
screen: `HASHTAG BLESSED.` → `THE FIRST WORDS OF THE SERMON.` → `IT STARTS WITH THE EMPTY-HANDED.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." This is the first of the Beatitudes. Matthew's Greek word for blessed is makarios: happy, fortunate, well off, the word Greeks used for the gods and the rich. Its Hebrew counterpart opens the book of Psalms: blessed is the man. So makarios is partly a congratulation. Lucky you. You're in a good place. Then look who he congratulates. The Greek word for poor here isn't a little short this month. It's the word for a beggar, someone with empty hands. Luke's version just says blessed be ye poor. Matthew adds in spirit, and Christians read that in more than one way. Some hear the humble: people who know they can't earn their way to God. Others hear the poor who have no pride left to hold on to. Some read both together. Either way, it's the opposite of self-sufficient. And the promise isn't someday. Theirs is the kingdom of heaven: present tense. Here's a picture that helps. You can't receive a gift with your hands full. Clutching your phone, your coffee and your bags, you have to put something down first. The poor in spirit already have their hands open. Maybe that's why this beatitude comes first. Everything else in the sermon is a gift, and empty hands can take it.
screen: `MAKARIOS: BLESSED, FORTUNATE.` · `POOR: A BEGGAR'S EMPTY HANDS.` · `IN SPIRIT: TWO READINGS.` · `THEIRS IS THE KINGDOM, NOW.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms open, facing up. Quietly name one thing you can't do on your own right now, help you need and haven't asked for, something you can't fix; no shame in it, your open hands already say I don't have everything. If you pray, you can bring that need to God with your hands open.
Blessed. Makarios in Greek: fortunate, well off, congratulations. And Jesus says it first to the poor in spirit.
Your line: empty hands can receive. The sermon starts with the empty-handed. Day two hundred thirty-three, done.

set apart and made holy by a priest's prayer
rewarded by God for living a good, clean life

fork.reveal: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." it starts with the empty-handed.

234.title: Those who mourn (Matthew 5:4)
234.hook: blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted
234.howItsDone: Christians keep funerals and memorial prayers for the dead, and some churches hold services for those grieving, especially around All Souls' Day or in the dark weeks before Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sermon's first word, blessed: fortunate, a congratulation for the empty-handed. Your line was empty hands can receive.

Grief gets a polite schedule. A few days off work. A card. Then, gently, the world expects a person to be fine. People say stay strong, or at least they're in a better place, and mean it kindly. But sometimes a grieving person needs someone who will let them be sad. The second line of Jesus's sermon goes somewhere few would expect. After the empty-handed, he congratulates the people who are crying.
screen: `GRIEF ON A POLITE SCHEDULE.` → `STAY STRONG.` → `THE SECOND LINE OF THE SERMON.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." The Greek word for mourn, pentheo, is used for mourning the dead: grief that shows, not a quiet sigh. Jesus doesn't say, blessed are those who get over it. Christians have read this in a few ways. Grief for someone you've lost. Grief over the wrong in the world, and over your own wrongs, as some early Christian teachers read it. And the prophet Isaiah had promised one who would come to comfort all that mourn. Jesus seems to be saying: that's now. The second word worth opening is comforted. In Greek it's a form of parakaleo, which can mean to call to your side. It's the same family as the word John's Gospel uses for the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, which the King James Bible translates the Comforter. So this comfort isn't a pat on the back from across the room. It's someone called in to sit beside you. And notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say you won't mourn, or that your grief is wrong or weak. Jesus himself wept at the tomb of his friend Lazarus. Paul later tells Christians not to sorrow as others which have no hope: not to stop sorrowing, but to sorrow with hope. That's the beatitude: grief that is real, and comfort promised to it.
screen: `MOURN: GRIEF FOR THE DEAD.` · `FOR THE LOST, AND FOR THE WRONG.` · `COMFORT: CALLED TO YOUR SIDE.` · `GRIEF WITH HOPE.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL BE COMFORTED.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you know who has lost something this year: a person, a marriage, a job, their health. Don't plan a speech; just ask what it would look like to sit beside them: a message that says I'm thinking of you, no reply needed, a meal, a walk. If you pray, you can name them before God.
Pentheo, the Greek word for mourn, grief that shows. The second beatitude: the ones who grieve out loud are blessed, because someone will come to their side.
Your line: mourning is not the end. Comfort is promised to grief, not to getting over it. See you tomorrow.

to beg out loud for help in a time of need
to sit in silence and fast after a hard loss

235.title: The meek (Matthew 5:5)
235.hook: meek means strength held gently, not weakness
235.howItsDone: Christians often name meekness, or gentleness, among the virtues they pray for; Paul lists it as a fruit of the Spirit, and many Christians practice it as holding back anger and not insisting on their own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pentheo: grief that shows, and comfort that comes to your side. Your line was mourning is not the end.

Nobody puts meek on a resume. It sounds like the kid who gets his lunch money taken: mousy, timid, a pushover. Meek and mild. In most offices, the meek don't inherit anything; they get talked over in meetings. So the third line of the sermon lands strangely. The meek are blessed, and not only that: they're going to inherit the whole earth. Either the world has meek wrong, or the sermon does.
screen: `NOBODY PUTS MEEK ON A RESUME.` → `MEEK AND MILD.` → `THEY'LL INHERIT THE EARTH?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth." This isn't new. It's almost word for word from Psalm 37: "But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace." In that psalm, the meek don't fret about the wicked getting ahead, and don't grab for themselves; they wait for God. The Greek word is praus. Greek writers used it for a gentle person, and for a wild animal tamed: a horse that has learned to take the bridle. A tamed horse isn't weak. It's every bit as strong as before; its strength is just under control, not thrashing around. That's meek: strength, held gently. Look who the Bible calls meek. Moses, of all people: the book of Numbers says he was very meek, above all the men on the face of the earth. The man who stood up to Pharaoh. And Jesus says of himself, I am meek and lowly in heart: the same Jesus who turned over tables in the temple. So meek can't mean spineless. It's someone who could hit back and doesn't; who could take and doesn't; who doesn't need to win every argument to know who they are. And the promise: they shall inherit the earth. Inherit is a gift word. You don't seize an inheritance; it's given to you. The grabbers take and take. The meek receive.
screen: `FROM PSALM 37.` · `PRAUS: A HORSE THAT TAKES THE BRIDLE.` · `MOSES, VERY MEEK.` · `INHERIT: GIVEN, NOT SEIZED.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL INHERIT THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Think of the person who most easily gets under your skin, and picture the moment they say the thing that sets you off; feel the sharp reply already loaded, and its strength. Now hold it, the way a rider holds the reins: not swallowing it forever, just not letting it bolt. If you pray, you can ask for gentleness.
Meek. Praus in Greek: not weak, but gentle strength, like a strong horse that takes the bridle.
Your line: strength, held gently. Meek was never the same as weak. That's day two hundred thirty-five.

quiet and shy, easily pushed around by others
angry inside but too scared to say so

236.title: Hungry for right (Matthew 5:6)
236.hook: blessed are those who hunger and thirst for what is right
236.howItsDone: Christians pursue righteousness both in personal prayer and repentance and in works of justice and charity: food banks, advocacy for the poor, and giving, which Christians in different churches see as part of the same calling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meek: strength held gently, like a horse that takes the bridle.

Hungry. Not a little peckish at four o'clock. Really hungry: a long hike, a fast, a day when everything went wrong and nobody remembered to eat. Or thirsty on a hot day, when water is the only thought left. The whole body leans toward one thing. Few things in a life get wanted like that: a person, a home, a cure, a child who comes back. The fourth line of the sermon names one more, and you can't eat it.
screen: `REALLY HUNGRY.` → `THIRSTY ON A HOT DAY.` → `WANTED LIKE WATER.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled." Righteousness can sound like a stiff, churchy word, even a little smug. But the Greek word, dikaiosune, is bigger and warmer. It means being right with God, and it also means justice: things set right between people. Greek uses one word for both. So does Hebrew: tsedakah, which is also the word Jews use for giving to the poor. So Jesus's listeners could hear both: a heart right with God, and a world where the widow gets fed and the worker gets paid. The prophet Amos put it like this: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Christians have leaned one way or the other at different times, and some hold both together: personal holiness and public justice. Now notice the verbs. Not blessed are the righteous. Blessed are the hungry for it: people who don't have it yet, who ache for it the way you ache for water. Nobody has to be finished. The blessing is on the wanting. And the promise: they shall be filled. The Greek word for filled, chortazo, is the one Matthew uses again when the crowds in the wilderness eat the loaves and fish and are filled. Not a taste. A full meal.
screen: `DIKAIOSUNE: RIGHT, AND JUSTICE.` · `LIKE A MIGHTY STREAM.` · `BLESSED ARE THE HUNGRY FOR IT.` · `FILLED: A FULL MEAL.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL BE FILLED.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that isn't right: something big, like hunger, a war, an injustice in the news, or something close, like a family rift, a friend treated unfairly, something you did. Don't argue with it; just feel the hunger for it to be made right, and notice where you feel it in your body. If you pray, you can offer that hunger to God.
Righteousness. Dikaiosune in Greek: being right with God and things set right between people, one word for both.
Your line: hunger for good. Right with God and right between people: one word, one hunger. Until tomorrow.

keeping every religious rule perfectly and strictly
feeling morally better than the people around you

237.title: The merciful (Matthew 5:7)
237.howItsDone: Kyrie eleison, Lord have mercy, is sung or said in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran worship, and Catholic and other Christians practice the works of mercy: feeding the hungry, visiting the sick and prisoners, and forgiving wrongs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, righteousness: right with God and justice, in one word. Your line was hunger for good.

A car cuts in front of another. In seconds, a whole biography gets written for the other driver: selfish, entitled, probably always like this. Now flip it. When you're the one cutting in, the story changes: late, a confusing lane, didn't see them. Mercy for yourself comes easily; for everyone else it gets rusty. Some readers notice a turn in the sermon here. The first four beatitudes describe people in need: empty hands, grief, meekness, hunger. The next ones describe what people give. And the first thing given is mercy.
screen: `CUT OFF IN TRAFFIC.` → `MERCY FOR YOURSELF.` → `NOW THE SERMON TURNS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy." The Greek word for mercy is eleos. If you've ever heard a church sing Kyrie eleison, that's the same word: Lord, have mercy. In the Bible, mercy is something you do with your hands, not only something you feel. In the story of the Good Samaritan, the neighbor is the one who showed mercy: he stopped, and bandaged. Behind it is a rich Hebrew world. One Hebrew word, chesed, means steady, loyal love that doesn't quit. Another, rachamim, shares its root with the Hebrew word for womb: the love a mother feels for the child she carried. Not a judge grudgingly letting you off. A mother's gut. The prophet Micah summed up what God asks: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God." Now the promise: they shall obtain mercy. It isn't a trade, as if you could buy God's mercy with your own. Christian teachers say God's mercy comes first. But there's a loop in it. Later, Jesus tells a story about a servant forgiven a huge debt who throws a fellow servant in prison over a small one. When the master hears, he hands the unforgiving servant back to his debt. Christians read it this way: mercy isn't earned, but mercy received is meant to flow on, and a heart that refuses to give it closes itself to receiving it.
screen: `ELEOS: KYRIE ELEISON.` · `CHESED AND RACHAMIM.` · `TO LOVE MERCY.` · `MERCY RECEIVED FLOWS ON.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL OBTAIN MERCY.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've judged recently, a coworker, a relative, a stranger, a public figure, and write in your mind the generous version of their story, the one you'd write for yourself: maybe they're exhausted, maybe scared, maybe they didn't see. You don't have to excuse anything; just let their story be as complicated as yours. If you pray, you can pray the old words, Lord, have mercy, for them and for you.
Mercy. Eleos in Greek, as in Kyrie eleison; in Hebrew, loyal love and a mother's tenderness. The fifth beatitude.
Your line: mercy returns. The fifth beatitude, and the turn from needing to giving. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

pity felt from a distance for someone weak

238.title: The pure in heart (Matthew 5:8)
238.hook: the pure in heart shall see God
238.howItsDone: Some Christians pray for a clean heart in the words of Psalm 51, and practices like examining the conscience, confession and silent prayer are meant to gather a scattered heart back to one center.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the merciful: mercy you do with your hands, meant to flow on. Your line was mercy returns. Today ends the first week on the mountain.

Count the tabs open on your screen right now. Or in your head. A lot of life happens in split screen: listening to a friend while checking a phone, eating while scrolling, praying while making the grocery list. It's rare to be all in one place. The sixth line of the sermon makes a startling promise: some people will see God. And it says who: not the smartest, not the most religious. The pure in heart.
screen: `COUNT THE OPEN TABS.` → `SPLIT SCREEN.` → `SOME WILL SEE GOD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God." Pure sounds like spotless, never done anything wrong. But the Greek word, katharos, is more like clean, clear, unmixed. Greek writers could use it of clean water, of metal with no alloy, of grain with the chaff winnowed out. And heart, in the Bible, isn't just feelings. It's the center of a person: where you think, choose and want. So a pure heart is an unmixed one. A single heart, not divided between God and ten other things, not saying one thing and wanting another. A psalm asked long ago: "Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart." In the nineteenth century, the Danish writer Soren Kierkegaard called a book Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. That's close. And the promise: they shall see God. Christians understand that in more than one way. Some look first to a final vision of God, face to face. Others also say the pure in heart start seeing God now, in a face, in bread, in a quiet morning, because they're finally looking in one direction. Look back at this first week on the mountain. Jesus sat down, then blessed the empty-handed, the mourners, the meek, the hungry for good, the merciful, and now the single-hearted. Each one is a way of being open.
screen: `KATHAROS: CLEAN, CLEAR, UNMIXED.` · `THE HEART: THE CENTER OF A PERSON.` · `TO WILL ONE THING.` · `SEEING GOD, THEN AND NOW.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL SEE GOD.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, do only one thing: breathe. When your mind opens another tab, and it will, notice it, close it gently, and come back to the breath; wandering isn't failing, the practice is the coming back. If you pray, you can offer this one undivided moment to God.
Katharos, the Greek word for clean, clear, unmixed. A single heart, not split ten ways, and the promise that it shall see God.
Your line: a single heart sees. Pure means unmixed, not spotless. That's one week on the mountain, done.

spotless, with no wrong ever done in your whole life
bright and shining, glowing with a heavenly light
